Thus, we expected individuals to perceive heightened demands and depleted resources in relation to social change, compared to the status quo. In the present study, we examined these potential demands and related resources using both surveybased and speech-coded measures, and their effect on physiological responses.

Current Study

Building on psychological evidence of a gap between progressive ideals and behavior, as well as physiological evidence of threat responses to social change, the present study examined whether expressing one's opinion about a hierarchy-disruptive social change elicited cardiovascular threat responses, even among its supporters. The social change under examination was an academic boycott-like initiative. We developed such experimental manipulation with inspiration from contemporary social movements, specifically the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) campaign (Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel [PACBI], n.d.) and the Shell Must Fall campaign (CODE ROOD, n.d.). The real-world relevance of this topic was particularly salient because data collection took place just weeks before campus protests and occupations in which students demanded that the university implement an academic boycott targeting both the fossil fuel industry and Israeli academic institutions.

Participants' physiological responses were assessed alongside political orientation and attitudes toward change, measured through both survey and speech coding. We further analyzed survey-and speech-based indicators of demands and resources to explore how individuals navigate conflicting motivations underlying support (and opposition) to change. We identified clusters based on speech-coded attitude, demands, and resources about social change and examined their differences in physiological threat and challenge responses. We included this qualitative component in line with Dixon et al. (2017), who argue that qualitative data are essential for understanding how individuals make sense of and navigate policy-related "political dilemmas," particularly when personal principles and behavioral implications are in tension. From their perspective, policy attitudes are not treated as direct reflections of stable internal beliefs, but as situated, action-oriented accounts through which individuals justify and negotiate potentially conflicting motivations, which are more difficult to measure using survey measures.

Finally, we explored the effects of threat and challenge responses, and speech-coded support on action intentions, via a short open question.

Our preregistered hypotheses were as follows: (1) Compared to maintaining the status quo, social change elicits stronger threat responses, even when accounting for political orientation and attitudes toward change; (2) this effect is mediated by the extent to which perceived demands outweigh available resources.

Our exploratory preregistered analyses focused on: (1) the qualitative content of speech-coded demands and resources; (2) whether expressed support and threat and challenge responses influence action intentions.

Given the multidimensionality of demands, resources, and social change itself, we also explored whether framing one's speech at the personal, ingroup, or systemic level would influence threat and challenge responses. To test this, we included a between-subject manipulation of speech focus (level of change). However, this manipulation did not function as intended; therefore, this factor was not included in the following analyses. Full methodological details and results regarding this manipulation are reported in https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd (section 7).

Methods

The preregistration (OSF Preregistration) included hypotheses, design, planned sample size, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and planned analyses.

Participants

To determine sample size requirements, we conducted an a-priori power analysis, using G*Power 3.0.10 (Faul et al., 2007) for the within-subject, and within-subject × between-subject interactions. To achieve a power of .90 at α = 0.05, assuming a medium effect size (f = .20), the analysis indicated a minimum sample size of 64 participants for the within-subjects effects and 84 participants for the 2 (within-subjects) × 3 (between-subjects) interaction. We collected responses among students at a large West-European university between March and June 2023.

Ultimately, 90 cases with valid data were collected. We paid participants €12,00. The sample's political orientation was slightly skewed toward the left (M = 5.00 on a 7-point scale, with 'extreme right' and 'extreme left' as endpoints; SD = 1.18; Sk = -.71). The average age of the final sample was 22 years old (SD = 3.14). The majority of participant came from western (n = 61; 67,8%) and eastern (n = 10; 11.1%) Europe, followed by east Asia (n = 5; 5.6%), South Africa (n = 3; 3.3%), Caribbean (n = 2; 2.2%), Latin America (n = 2; 2,2%), the Middle-east (n = 2; 2.2%), South Asia (n = 2; 2.2%), North America (n=2; 2,2%), and Southeast Asia (n=1; 1.1%). Regarding minority status, 27 people identified as BIPoC, 33 as LGBTQ+, 63 as women, and 28 as working class or low middle class. The sample's average (family) income was between €50,000 and €80,000 (M = 3.55, SD = 1.70) and slightly skewed toward lower incomes.

Design

We used a 2 (state of change: status quo; social change) x 3 (level of change: system; ingroup; personal) mixed design with repeated measures on the first factor. State of change was not randomized for theoretical and ecological reasons, as social change is typically interpreted relative to a stable status quo (de la Sablonnière, 2017), suggesting that the status quo condition should be presented first to establish a common reference point across participants and minimize variability due to differences in prior knowledge of the social change topic.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions of level of change. However, as aforementioned, level of change was left out from following analyses.

Procedure

Participants first completed a 10-minute online survey in their own time, measuring political orientation, their attitudes towards eco-justice, and neoliberal capitalism. The online survey closed with demographic questions regarding age, nationality, ethnicity, sex assigned at birth, gender identity, sexual orientation, income, socioeconomic class identity, mental and physical disability, and faculty of study. Between 24 and 48 hours after completing the survey, participants attended their scheduled laboratory session, which was conducted in the psychophysiology lab at the Science Park of the university. Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machine and then completed a computer task. During the task, participants first read about the status quo scenario. They then delivered a one-minute speech about their personal opinion on the reading, which was recorded via a microphone. The speech was followed by a manipulation check, and the threat and challenge appraisal scales (see below). This procedure was then repeated a second time for the social change condition.

Material

Complete materials and scoring procedures are available in OSF (https://osf.io/yxvd3/overview?view_only=25061cf09f5449899da4b39515994ce8).

Materials for the manipulation of state of change, survey demands and resources, and support of change variables are also available in https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd (section 2).

Manipulation of State of Change

Participants were presented with a text describing the status quo, followed by a text describing the social change. We opted for a topic of social change that was relevant for students at our university at the time, while being novel enough to reduce differences in prior knowledge effects: Collaborations between Dutch Academia and external stakeholders.

In the status quo condition, participants read about the "open collaboration model," and in the social change condition participants read about the "selective collaboration model".

While these names were created for the purposes of the study, we designed both scenarios to closely reflect real-world practices. The open collaboration model reflected the university's current approach, which emphasizes partnerships with a wide range of external entities: A strategy the university promotes on its official website. In contrast, the selective collaboration Instability, disruption, and novelty are considered main characteristics of social change (de la Sablonnière, 2017). Thus, in the status quo condition, the social relations between the groups involved (i.e., students, academia, external parties) were described as stable ("This has been the case for a very long time, as Dutch academia follows the 'Open collaboration model'") and long-standing yet impactful ("These long-standing collaborations have a big impact on the university").

In the social change condition, we introduced a disruption of the normative structure of Dutch academia ("They [changing collaboration model] will contribute to reshape finances, quality, characteristics, moral value, and amount of opportunities seen today in the university education and research"), as well as a somewhat rapid pace of change ("According to different sources, it is very likely that change is about to happen at this university and Dutch academia").

Change was framed as unstable ("These changing collaborations are expected to have a very big impact at Utrecht university") and unprecedented ("This is unprecedented for Dutch academia, and it will fall under the new 'selective collaboration model").

Finally, we included real-world examples of collaborations involving parties such as NGOs, Shell, Unilever, KPMG, and ABN Amro. This aimed to enhance the ecological validity of our manipulation while highlighting the complexity of the issue, which involved both benefits (e.g., job opportunities) and controversies (e.g., workers' rights violations).

Additionally, tailoring the content to the participants, the texts emphasized activities crucial to students, such as "securing internship opportunities," and "setting-up study programs". By providing this context, we ensured that individuals could form a more informed opinion based on a rounded understanding of the topic.

Manipulation Check of State of Change.

We evaluated the effectiveness of our manipulation of state of change through a single item, asking participant to rate whether the text they read suggested that "…drastic changes were about to take place in the Netherlands." This approach, while abstract, was chosen so that the measure could be applied consistently across all three experimental conditions.

Physiological Measurements

We assessed cardiovascular markers for engagement, threat and challenge responses based on established physiological markers (see Seery, 2013). The protocols for physiological data collection and scoring can be found here: https://osf.io/k5gjq/. Engagement reflects the degree of sympathetic nervous system activation, indicated by increases in heart rate (HR) and decreases in pre-ejection period (PEP). Pre-ejection period is a measure of ventricular contractility (VC) and represents the interval between the start of the electromechanical systole (as indicated by the Q-point in the ECG) and the opening of the aorta valve (as indicated by the B-point in the ICG).

Once engaged, individuals may exhibit a challenge or threat cardiovascular profile.

Challenge responses are characterized by relatively high cardiac output (CO) and low total peripheral resistance (TPR), reflecting efficient heart function and vasodilation. In contrast, threat responses involve relatively low or stable CO combined with relatively high TPR, indicating vasoconstriction and reduced cardiac efficiency.

To capture these physiological responses, we continuously recorded impedance cardiography (ICG), electrocardiography (ECG), and blood pressure (BP) throughout the entire lab session using a Biopac MP150 system (Biopac Systems Inc., Goleta, CA). To ensure the quality of the physiological data, two experimenters supervised each lab session.

Impedance cardiography is a noninvasive technique for measuring stroke volume (SV) and systolic time intervals (e.g., pre-ejection period; PEP, see Sherwood et al., 1990). Stroke volume, which was determined here using the Kubicek formula (see Sherwood et al., 1990), represents the amount of blood that the heart pumps in one heartbeat. Multiplying SV with heart rate (derived from the ECG) yields Cardiac Output (CO; i.e., the amount of blood in liters that the heart pumps per minute).

To measure ICG, we used the Biopac NICO100c module and four spot-electrodes, two of which were placed at the back of the neck, and two on the back, 30cm apart from each other.

The two outer electrodes inject a small (400μA) alternating current while the two inner electrodes measure the voltage developed through the thorax volume. As output the NICO100c provides measures of baseline impedance (Z0) and the rate of change in impedance (dZ/dt), which can be used to derive measures of cardiac performance (stroke volume, pre-ejection period; see Sherwood et al., 1990).

To measure electrocardiography, we used the ECG100 module and a Lead I electrode configuration (one electrode at the base of the throat, another one four fingers above the last left rib).

To measure blood pressure, we used the NIBP100d module, which is equipped with a finger cuff placed over the index and middle fingers of the non-dominant hand to measure the pulse wave. The NIBP100d provides a measure of mean arterial pressure (MAP), which, in combination with CO, is used to calculate TPR using the formula: TPR = (MAP/CO) × 80. For one participant, CV measures could not be accurately calculated due to electrode detachment during the experimental session and were therefore excluded from analyses pertaining to physiological measures. Physiological data was stored using Acqknowledge (Version 5.0.8.1; BIOPAC Systems, Inc., 2023) and scored using the PhysioData Toolbox (Sjak-Shie, 2022). For analysis, cardiovascular data were segmented the final minute of the 5-minute baseline period (during which participant watched a relaxing video) and the two 1-minute speech task periods. The physiological data were manually cleaned, scored, and examined for influential cases by two independent coders, who then met to resolve any major discrepancies.

Following the reactivity approach, we calculated difference scores by subtracting baseline values from task period values. These difference scores served as the variables in our statistical models. Finally, we calculated a unified Threat and Challenge Index (TCI) by adding the standardized cardiac output (CO) scores to the inverted standardized total peripheral resistance (TPR) scores (i.e., TPR z-scores multiplied by -1), such that higher values reflect a greater challenge response, and lower values reflect a greater threat response.

In addition to this relative cardiovascular reactivity approach (which is the current standard in research on the BPS-CT), in the https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd section 7).

Speech Task About Social Change and Speech-Coded Demands and Resources

Participants were asked to deliver a one-minute speech about their thoughts and feelings regarding the collaboration model that was described in the text they read. The guiding question invited them to focus on the possible consequences of the collaboration model. Their speeches were automatically transcribed using AmberScript, and then manually coded along the following dimensions, using NVivo (version 14; Lumivero, 2023) and Microsoft Excel.

Speech Coding of Support. Using a scale from 1 ("Very non-supportive") to 7 ("Very supportive"), we coded the extent to which participants supported the open collaboration model in the status quo condition, and the selective collaboration model in the social change condition.

A score of 1 indicated clear opposition, 2 indicated strong opposition while acknowledging some positive aspects, 3 indicated moderate opposition or reservations, 4 indicated neither support nor opposition, 5 indicated moderate support while expressing some doubts or reservations, 6 indicated strong support with minor reservations, and 7 indicated unequivocal support. As coding progressed, we further refined the operational criteria used to distinguish between categories. In particular, we distinguished between general evaluations of the model (e.g., describing it as "good" or "bad") and explicit expressions of support for its implementation. Explicit statements endorsing implementation were given greater weight because they more directly captured participants' support for the proposed model. For example, statements such as "I support this" or "I fully support this" were coded as stronger evidence of support than general positive evaluations of the model.

Speech Coding of Demands and Resources.

Two independent coders analyzed participants' speeches using iterative thematic coding. Our approach was grounded in the appraisal component of the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (Blascovich & Mendes, 2000) and followed reflexive thematic analysis guidelines (Braun & Clarke, 2008).

The aim was to identify perceived demands and resources in participants' views on social change, with demands referring to obstacles, risks, or pressures, and resources reflecting assets, support, or capabilities that help individuals cope with or succeed in implementing the selective collaboration model. The first coder identified key types of demands and resources using a combination of bottom-up coding and theoretical guidance. Each speech was reviewed to label segments reflecting these categories, and constant comparison techniques were used to group similar codes into broader themes. Participants worried about losing personal and ingroup privileges such as funding, internships, and opportunities tied to the current system.

"These collaborations, if they end, they will have effect on all of us because first of all, we will get probably less internship opportunities, less fundings, maybe the tuition fees are going to be higher because the university itself gets less fundings."

Value-interest conflict (34)

Participants experienced tension between endorsing (vague) progressive ideals and managing the practical consequences of the academic boycott.

"Whilst I support civility and definitely hate the actions of big companies like ABN AMRO, I am a bit nervous and afraid to see how this will affect the curriculum of several studies."

Total (175)

The final coding framework comprised three main demands (implementation concerns, status loss, value-interest conflict) and four main resources (moral compass, instrumental support, moral support, rationalizations) (see Tables 1 and 2). After finalizing the coding framework, two coders independently coded the speeches, counting the instances in which each demand and resource were mentioned by participants. For each coded category of demands and resources, the count per participant generally ranged from 0 to 5.

Description Example

Moral compass (167)

Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by viewing it as morally necessary and urgent, focusing on longterm benefits despite the sacrifices involved.

"But we all have to make, like, sacrifices. We all have to do."

Instrumental support ( 23)

Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by relying on institutional and community practical support.

"I think that's easily manageable for the university if these changes are planned properly in time and not just improvised."

Moral support (66)

Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by drawing on the collective's ethical leadership and shared community values, emphasizing collective responsibility toward change.

"So I think they should do everything they can […], because everyone in the Western world, everyone in the world has a part to play in that."

Rationalizations (20)

Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by employing various rationalizations, heuristics, and cognitive biases to explain their reluctance toward change.

"So I think collaboration should continue, but some restrictions should be there. I'm not saying that no restriction at all, but they should continue collaborating."

Total (276)

We finally assessed interrater reliability for the seven coded demands and resources using a two-way random-effects model with absolute agreement intraclass correlation. The ICCs ranged from .70 to .97 (all ps < .001), indicating good to excellent reliability across codes (ten Hove et al., 2024). As a final step, to improve the quality and accuracy of the coding, the two coders met to discuss and resolve few major disagreements (see https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd

https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd section 2 for details).

Survey Demands and Resources Appraisal

Participants self-reported how they appraised the demands and resources associated with each collaboration model. To assess demands (α = .65 for status quo; α = .60 for social change), we used in total six items capturing perceived effort and uncertainty across three To assess resources (α = .60 for status quo; α = .71 for social change), a total of six items measured perceived ability and support at the same levels. For instance: "I feel that I can deal with the existence of the 'open collaboration model' at the university" (personal ability), and "I feel that Dutch academia will receive support to deal with the introduction of the 'selective collaboration model'" (system-level support).

Scores for the demands and resources scales were calculated separately by averaging the items within each scale. Higher values indicated greater demands and greater resources, respectively.

Political Orientation

We measure political orientation using a single 7-point Likert scale item, where one endpoint indicated 'far right' and the other 'far left'.

Attitudes Toward Social Change

We selected attitude measures that were theoretically linked to our manipulation of social change, thus focusing on sustainability, human rights, and neoliberalism, to further test whether threat persists among supporters of change.

Eco-justice.

Attitudes toward eco-justice and sustainability were measured using six items developed ad hoc for this study. The scale captured concerns about natural resource consumption ("In the Netherlands, too little attention is paid to how many natural resources we consume") and CO₂ emissions ("Dutch society has reached the point where CO₂ emissions are under control"; reverse-coded), as well as about climate racism and eco-colonialism ("The Netherlands should teach developing countries how to become more sustainable"; reversecoded). For analyses, we used the overall mean score across all six items (α = .80), reflecting general ecojustice attitudes.

Neoliberalism. Attitudes toward neoliberalism were measured using 11 items developed ad hoc for this study. The scale reflected aspects related to redistribution and public ownership ("In the Netherlands, basic services such as health care and public transport should be public and provided to everyone, free of charge"), and others related to free-market principles, such as competition and private ownership ("Competition in the Dutch economy is good because it stimulates innovation"; reverse-coded). For analyses, we used the overall mean score across all 10 items (α = .79), reflecting general opposition to neoliberal capitalism.

Acton Intentions

To explore whether threat and challenge responses influence action intentions, participants were asked at the end of the study to write up to 200 characters describing whether they would take action in relation to the selective collaboration model, and if so, what action.

We opted for this measure due to time constraints and to gain initial insight into how participants spontaneously conceive action in relation to progressive social change.

These brief responses were subsequently coded on a five-point ordinal scale, where 1 indicated no action (n = 15), 2 indicated that others should take action (n = 31), 3 indicated awareness raising (n = 11), 4 indicated individual action (n = 9), and 5 indicated collective action (n = 24). Notably, 46 participants (51.11%) reported a willingness to take action, suggesting a potential overreporting of action intentions compared to findings from general surveys (OECD, 2024).

Analysis Plan

To test our hypotheses, we fitted three linear mixed-effects models (MLMs) examining the effects of state of change (status quo vs. social change; Level 1) on cardiovascular challenge-threat responses (CO, TPR, and TCI), while accounting for repeated observations nested within participants (Level 2). Models were estimated using maximum likelihood (ML; REML = FALSE) in R using the lme4 package (version 1.1-37; Bates et al., 2015) and included participant-specific random intercepts to account for the dependence among repeated observations. Random slopes were not estimated because each participant contributed only two observations. Following the default specification in lme4, level-1 residuals were assumed to be independent and homoscedastic, with a common residual variance estimated across observations. To examine whether threat also emerges among supporters of change, we sequentially added main and moderation effects between state of change and political orientation, eco-justice attitudes, neoliberalism attitudes, and speech-coded support.

Secondly, we planned to test whether the relationship between social change (vs. status quo) and threat and challenge responses was mediated by demands and resources using the multilevel mediation approach described by Bauer et al. (2006). This approach combines the mediator and dependent variable into a single stacked response variable and estimates all mediation paths within one mixed-effects model. However, this analysis was not pursued further because the mediator did not significantly predict the outcome when included in the model.

To identify distinct participant profiles based on speech content and opinions on the academic boycott, we conducted a hierarchical cluster analysis (Ward's method, squared Euclidean distance) using z-scores of speech-coded support and demands, and resources. The number of clusters was determined via agglomeration coefficients and dendrogram inspection from the hierarchical analysis, and the solution was refined using k-means clustering to optimize cluster membership. We then ran one-way ANOVAs to test for differences in cardiac output (CO), total peripheral resistance (TPR), and Threat and Challenge Index (TCI) across clusters.

Finally, we explored whether physiological TCI and speech-coded support for social change predicted action intentions using logistic regressions, and whether clusters differed in terms of action intentions using X² tests. We additionally examined whether cardiovascular challenge-threat responses varied as a function of the level of change manipulation (i.e., whether participants were instructed to focus their reflection on themselves, their ingroup, or the system) by adding the interaction between state of change and level of change to our previous models predicting CO, TPR, and TCI. The results of these analyses are reported in the https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd

https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd (section 6), additional analyses examining the effects of minority status variables (i.e., gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation, and socioeconomic class) on cardiovascular challenge-threat responses.

Results

Manipulation Check of State of Change

A paired-sample t-test indicated that participants perceived more drastic change after reading about the social change compared to the status quo, t(89) = -16.16, p < .001. This indicated that we effectively manipulated a state of perceived change.

Cardiovascular Markers of Task Engagement

Paired sample t-test results indicated that, compared to baseline, HR increased in both the status quo, t(88) = -17.18, p < .001, and the social change, t(88) = -13.23, p < .001, conditions. Moreover, compared to baseline, PEP decreased significantly in both the status quo condition, t(88) = 4.91, p < .001, and the social change, t(88) = 3.00, p = .004, condition. This shows that our speech paradigm was able to establish sufficient engagement for a further examination of CO and TPR in terms of threat and challenge.

Effect of State of Change on Physiological Threat and Challenge

Following these preliminary analyses, we tested our pre-registered Hypothesis 1 using multilevel models on baseline-adjusted physiological reactivity scores. Unconditional mean models indicated substantial between-person variance for CO (ICC = .42), TPR (ICC = .47), and TCI (ICC = .44), supporting the use of multilevel modeling.

In line with our predictions, participants showed greater threat responses when speaking about the social change compared to the status quo, characterized by lower cardiac output (CO), β = -.67, 95% CI [-.85, -.49], p < .001 (Figure 1), higher total peripheral resistance (TPR), β = .44, 95% CI [.25, .63], p < .001 (Figure 2), and a lower threat-challenge index (TCI), β = -.61, 95% CI [-.79, -.43], p < .001 (Figure 3). Across all three models, the random intercepts indicated substantial between-participant variability in starting levels of cardiovascular responses. The estimated standard deviations of the random intercepts were 0.73 for CO, 0.72 for TPR, and 0.72 for TCI. The estimated residual standard deviations were 0.59 for CO, 0.65 for TPR, and 0.61 for TCI. Visual inspection of residual and Q-Q plots indicated no substantial violations of the assumptions of normality or homoscedasticity for any of the models. Predicted CO (and Standard Error Bar) by State of Social Change. Predicted TPR (and Standard Error Bar) by State of Social Change. Predicted TCI (and Standard Error Bar) by State of Social Change.

Across Figures 1 2 3, a consistent pattern emerges: on average, participants showed a relative tendency towards physiological challenge responses during the status quo speech. In contrast, average scores during the social change speech shifted toward a more threat response.

To be noted, however, individual responses varied in both conditions, with some participants exhibiting challenge responses and others showing threat responses regardless of the speech condition.

Cardiovascular Threat Among Supporters of Change

Descriptively, participants were, on average, moderately left-leaning (M = 5.00, SD = 1.18, on a 7-point scale), reported relatively positive eco-justice attitudes (M = 5.01, SD = 1.06), and expressed moderate opposition to neoliberal capitalism (M = 3.52, SD = 0.86). Mixedmodel effects further revealed that participants expressed stronger support for the academic boycott (M = 5.40, SD = 1.46) than for the status quo (M = 3.19, SD = 1.18), β = 1.35, 95% CI [1.13, 1.58], p < .001.

To test whether social change elicited threat even among its supporters, we examined whether the effects of state of change on CO, TPR, and TCI were moderated by political orientation, eco-justice attitudes, neoliberal capitalism attitudes, and expressed support for social change. Multilevel models included the corresponding main effects and their interactions with state. Across all outcomes, state of change remained a significant predictor of lower CO and TCI, and higher TPR (all ps < .001). Importantly, none of the interaction terms reached statistical significance (all ps ≥ .18), suggesting that the threatening effect of social change also persisted among its supporters. We nonetheless observed an association between neoliberal capitalism attitudes and cardiovascular responses, such that stronger endorsement of neoliberal capitalism was associated with higher challenge, including higher CO (β = .21, 95% CI [-.01, .44], p = .062), lower TPR (β = -.21, 95% CI [-.44, .02], p = .075), and higher TCI (β = .23, 95% CI [.01, .46], p = .043), suggesting that participants with more progressive economic attitudes actually experienced higher threat than their less progressive counterparts.

These findings revealed a striking tendency: At an explicit level, people were more positive about social change than about the status quo; however, at an implicit, cardiovascular, level people were more threatened when reflecting on social change than on the status quo, somewhat regardless of their political orientation, their attitudes toward political issues, and their expressed support of social change.

Sources of Threat and Challenge: Effects of Self-Reported Demands and Resources

Survey Demands and Resources

Contrary to our Hypothesis 2, we did not find that survey demands and resources mediated the relationship between state of change and TCI (see Supplementary Material

Chapter 3, section 6 for details). Somewhat in line with BPS-CT prediction and research (Seery, 2013), higher ingroup uncertainty correlated with a lower TCI (r = -.25; p = .018), suggesting that when a participant perceived their ingroup facing more uncertainties they may experience higher threat.

Expressed Demands and Resources

To further examine Hypothesis 2 and shed light on the different experiences people may have had when reflecting on social change, we then examined possible clusters based on speech-coded support for social change, demands, and resources. Hierarchical cluster analysis suggested that either a 3-or 4-cluster solution could be justified. Although the 3-cluster solution corresponded to a substantial increase in linkage distance around a rescaled distance of approximately 20-25, the 4-cluster solution identified at a slightly lower level, around 15-18, and allowed for greater differentiation among subgroups while still maintaining reasonable between-cluster separation. Thus, a 4-cluster solution was preferred. Such clusters are described below in order of support for social change, ranging from the most negative to the most positive. We report cluster averages and standard deviations for the demands and resources measures. All values should be interpreted relative to each measure's scale, so that labels such as "high" or "moderate" indicate levels within the context of that variable, rather than absolute magnitudes.

Interestingly, results from three one-way ANOVAs showed no significant differences between clusters in ecojustice attitudes (p = .511), neoliberalism attitudes (p = .061), or political orientation (p = .192).

Cluster 1: Rationalizing Opponents

Participants in this cluster (n = 11) showed opposition to the selective collaboration model (M = 2.64; SD = 1.21), paired with the highest use of rationalizations as resources (M = 1.82; SD = 0.60), and some value-interest conflict as a demand (M = 1.09; SD = 0.83). These patterns suggest that, rather than openly expressing opposition, participants whose responses fell in this cluster tried to rationalize or justify their stance, and at times to defend a moral selfimage.

Cluster 2: Ambivalent Supporters

Participants in this cluster (n = 21) showed moderate support for the selective collaboration model (M = 4.67; SD = 0.86), paired with high status loss (M = 1.90: SD = 0.77), and value-interest conflict (M = 1.05; SD = 0.97), but low resources across all types.

Participants in this cluster appeared to struggle with the tension between maintaining a progressive moral image and confronting the real consequences implied by social change.

Cluster 3: Concerned Moralists

Participants in this cluster (N = 44) showed high support for the selective collaboration model (M = 6.14; SD = 0.71), paired with the strongest moral compass (M = 2.77: SD = 1.05), high moral support (M = 1.02; SD = 1.05), and some implementation concerns (M = 0.89; SD = 1.28). Participants in this cluster were concerned about whether social change will achieve its intended outcomes, but they reaffirmed their support by appealing to moral reasoning and reframing of demands.

Cluster 4: Collective Resilients

Participants in this cluster (N = 14) showed the highest support for the selective collaboration model (M = 6.36; SD = 0.74), paired with the highest instrumental support (M = 1.50: SD = 0.65), high moral support (M = 1.00; SD = 0.88), and mid-low demands across all types. Participants in this cluster appear less concerned about the negative consequences of social change, while feeling supported and protected by the institutions and communities around them.

Threat and Challenge Responses Among Clusters

One-way ANOVAs showed significant differences on the threat-challenge index (TCI) among the four clusters, F(3, 85) = 10.43, p < .001, η² = 0.27 (Figure 4). Games-Howell post hoc comparisons indicated that ambivalent supporters showed the strongest threat response among all clusters (M = -1.73, SD = 2.05), and post-hoc tests confirmed that they differed significantly from every other group, namely collective resilients (d = 0.54, p < .001), rationalizing opponents (d = -1.05, p = .007), and concerned moralists (d = 0.68, p = .012). In contrast, collective resilients showed the strongest tendency towards challenge profile (M = 0.84, SD = 1.13), and significantly more so than concerned moralists (d = 1.29, p = .028), but not significantly different from rationalizing opponents (d = -0.71, p = .392). Rationalizing opponents (M = 0.05, SD = 1.23) exhibited a mild challenge response, while concerned moralists (M = -0.57, SD = 1.07) showed a mild threat response, with both clusters displaying relatively balanced distributions across threat and challenge categories. These two clusters did not differ significantly from one another (d = -1.56, p = .582).

Figure 4

Threat-Challenge Index (TCI) Responses to Social Change among Speech-based Clusters.

Action Intentions

Logistic regression results showed that neither TCI (β = .188, p = .212) nor speechcoded support for change (β = .0.86, p = .512) significantly predicted action intentions.

In an exploratory manner, we then tested differences in action intentions among the four clusters (Figure 5). Chi-square tests indicated a significant association between cluster and action type, X²(12) = 38.67, p < .001 (Monte Carlo p < .001). Collective resilients tended to report more collective action intentions (n = 7, 70%), whereas rationalizing opponents slightly favored individual action (n = 3, 30%). Concerned moralists appeared to lean toward collective action (n = 10, 37%) or indicated that others should act (n = 17, 63%). Ambivalent supporters were somewhat more likely to indicate no action (n = 7, 30%) or that others should act (n = 10, 43%). Importantly, although certain trends were observable, each cluster exhibited a variety of action types, indicating that these results are only indicative and not conclusive. This is further underscored by the uneven cluster sizes, which ranged from small (11) to large (44).

Proportion of Action Type per Cluster of Speech-coded Support, Demands, and Resources

Discussion

In the current research, we investigated whether systemic and progressive social change, in the form of an academic boycott of unsustainable and unethical collaboration partners, elicited a physiological threat response, even among supporters of change. To assess this, we tested whether the threat response persisted after controlling for the main and moderating effect of political orientation and survey and speech-coded attitudes toward change.

We additionally explored potential root causes of such threat responses, by looking at scale and speech-coded demands and resources, and whether physiological responses influenced action intentions.

In line with our pre-registered Hypothesis 1 we found that, compared to the status quo, participants in the social change condition displayed lower Cardiac Output (CO), increased Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR), and relatively low scores on a combined Threat and Challenge Index (TCI). All these results indicate a clear threat response to social change in the form of an academic boycott-like initiative targeting unsustainable and unethical collaborations. These were not moderated by political orientation and attitudes toward change and persisted when controlling for these variables. Importantly, participants expressed stronger support for social change compared to the status quo, suggesting a possible tension between expressed support and cardiovascular responses.

Contrary to Hypothesis 2, neither survey demands, nor survey resources predicted cardiovascular threat or challenge responses. Interestingly, however, we still found an association between increased perceived ingroup uncertainty and physiological threat, suggesting that the extent to which participants felt uncertain about their (academic) ingroup may be associated with physiological threat responses, in line with BPS-CT predictions. Finally, neither threat nor challenge responses, nor expressed support for social change, directly predicted action intentions measured through an open-ended question. Exploratory analyses tentatively suggested meaningful cluster differences: threatened clusters (ambivalent supporters and concerned moralists) tended toward inaction and delegation of responsibility, although concerned moralists expressed some collective action intentions; collective resilients reported more collective action intentions, whereas rationalizing showed action intentions comparable to concerned moralists without however delegating to others. These patterns should be interpreted as indicative rather than conclusive.

Theoretical and Practical Implications

Extending the Biopsychosocial Model to Hierarchy-Disruptive Social Change

Our findings provided initial empirical support for extending the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Blascovich & Mendes, 2010) into the domain of hierarchy-disruptive social change. Participants displayed prototypical threat physiology, namely lower cardiac output (CO) combined with increased total peripheral resistance (TPR), when reflecting on social change initiatives, and even when controlling for their political orientation, attitudes, and expressed support for the change. This tension between expressed support and physiological responses aligns with Seery's (2013) observation that subjective measures often fail to capture underlying motivational states. By integrating cardiovascular markers, we revealed hidden stress responses patterns that might have remained invisible using survey measures alone (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013). It further suggests that the threat posed by social change may persist even among those who support it. This may raise the possibility that responses to such changes depend not only on individuals' support for the change itself, but also on how they appraise the demands it creates relative to the resources they perceive as available to cope with them, as suggested by our cluster analyses and, to a lesser extent, our survey measures.

It should be noted that the survey, text, and physiological indices of challenge and threat differed in the precise targets of their appraisals, despite their relation to each other. That is, in the survey and text coding, demands and resources referred to an evaluation of the two respective collaboration models, while the physiological measures most directly refer to challenge and threat in the motivated performance situation, i.e., forming and expressing one's opinion on the two collaboration models. Still, we propose that these different appraisals, captured through self-reports and reflected in physiological measures of challenge and threat, were meaningfully related, as was suggested from the cluster analysis.

Indeed, speech content could be in a meaningful way related to demands (e.g., uncertainty, required effort) and resources (e.g., support) described by the BPS-CT. For example, uncertainty is an inherent aspect of social change and can operate as a negative "affective cue" (Blascovich & Mendes, 2000) feeding into a physiological threat response when reflecting on, and responding to, change. Moreover, ambivalent and rationalizing responses to social change may have been demanding because they required more effort than reflecting on the status quo. Finally, at the resource side of the appraisal part of the BPS-CT, feeling supported, i.e., knowing that one is not alone in one's opinion, may have fed into the relative challenge response among collective resilients.

Overall, we propose that a blend of different demand and resource factors, at different levels of analysis, possibly contributed to the physiological threat responses to social change, as well as to the substantial variation in this response as evident from the cluster analysis.

Indeed, it seems unlikely that the threat of social change as observed here would have been due to a single factor. For example, although required effort is likely to have been a central demand, if this would have been the only factor, one would have also expected stronger signs of engagement (HR, PEP) than were currently observed in the social change condition (see also Gendolla & Richter, 2010; Wright & Kirby, 2001). Still, despite that, a strong case can be made for the connection between the broader demands and resources of social change and the more specific demands and resources when expressing one's opinion on the change. We also note that future research should connect demands and resources at different levels of analysis of (the threat of) social change even more directly and explicitly than we were able to do here.

Notably, although meaningful differences in cardiovascular challenge and threat emerged across clusters characterized by distinct patterns of expressed demands and resources, survey-measures demands and resources did not mediate the relationship between state of change and cardiovascular responses. This suggests that the mechanisms underlying these physiological responses are only partially captured in our study. One explanation is methodological, as self-reports were collected after the speech task whereas cardiovascular responses were recorded during it, allowing for possible shifts over time. Alternatively, cardiovascular challenge and threat may reflect rapid or partially nonconscious appraisals not fully captured by retrospective self-report (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013).

Threat of Hierarchy-Disruptive Social Change

Our findings align with theoretical insight proposing that hierarchy-disruptive social changes are often experienced as stressful and destabilizing (De La Sablonnière, 2017) and, consistent with the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Seery, 2014), they can elicit physiological threat responses. Prior research has shown that challenges to traditional norms, hierarchical structures, or exposure to minoritized group members are particularly status-threatening for dominant group members and conservatives, resulting in heightened physiological stress (Long et al., 2025; Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; Scheepers & Knight, 2020). Extending this literature, the present study suggests that even individuals who outwardly support progressive social change can exhibit physiological signs of threat, maybe especially when their own or their ingroup's privileges or resources are perceived to be at risk, or when uncertainties and concerns arise regarding the implementation of social change.

This divergence from previous work may reflect our focus on systemic, ecologically grounded social movement-driven changes, rather than the more constrained intergroup competition paradigms commonly used in prior research. By situating participants within realistic scenarios of broad societal transformation, our approach may have enabled them to engage more directly with the complex material implications and tensions inherent in hierarchy-disruptive social change, making the demands and uncertainties associated with these changes salient even for those who supported them.

Our cluster analyses provide some tentative insight into why supporters may experience such threat. One possible explanation concerns potential losses to personal or ingroup privileges, together with tensions between endorsing social justice in principle and fearing the implications of change, as seen among ambivalent supporters. The uncertainty stemming from this tension may help explain their heightened threat responses (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010), as suggested also by the link found between survey-measured ingroup uncertainty and TCI.

This pattern aligns with Tosaka's (2024) argument that liberals who endorse justice in principle may nonetheless resist systemic interventions when those interventions require personal or group sacrifice. It also resonates with the notion of performative allyship (Kutlaca & Radke, 2022), and the evidence gathered about the attitude-implementation gap (Glasford, 2022), wherein symbolic support fails to translate into substantive action. Our findings suggest that this gap may at times be driven by an unresolved conflict between endorsing abstract values and confronting the costly realities of progress. Regardless of intentions, vague ideals could prove hollow, potentially contributing to the delegation of responsibility to others, which may give the appearance of progress while leaving the status quo largely intact.

Threat, although lower, was also observed among concerned moralists, who tended to frame potential losses as moral imperatives. Unlike the vague ideals observed in ambivalent supporters, these moral imperatives were more concrete and were accompanied by greater acceptance of the costly reality of progress. This more concrete framing may partly account for the presence of some collective action intentions among this cluster, alongside delegating responsibility to others. While these findings are tentative, they are broadly consistent with the idea that moral obligation, rooted in deeply shared values, strongly motivates collective action (Ellemers et al., 2019; Sabucedo et al., 2018; Uysal et al., 2022). Related research on utopian thinking likewise showed that envisioning more just futures can elicit hope, reduce system justification, and strengthen intentions to act (Badaan et al., 2022; Badaan et al., 2020). Overall, although moral imperatives seem more motivating than vague ideals, they may still be insufficient to drive sustained collective action, bringing further nuance to previous work on the role of morality in social change.

Taken together, our cluster analyses suggest that individuals may occupy intermediate psychological positions during periods of systemic change, simultaneously supporting progressive reforms while experiencing threat arising from anticipated losses, uncertainty, and competing values. Although these findings remain preliminary, they suggest the possibility that threat may not simply distinguish supporters from opponents of hierarchy-disruptive social change. Rather, it may represent a partially common, though different in content, response to the demands of systemic change, even among those who ultimately endorse it. Our findings may also suggest that the implications of threat may depend on how it is navigated. While ambivalent supporters appeared to remain caught between abstract commitments to justice and concerns about the costs of change, concerned moralists likewise exhibited physiological threat but were more likely to frame those costs as morally necessary and expressed at least some willingness to engage in collective action. This pattern suggests that experiencing threat need not always be incompatible with supporting or acting toward social change. Threat may not be interpreted as inherently and absolutely negative (or positive). Rather than something to be avoided in the interest of social harmony (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018), it may represent a recurring feature of systemic change (de la Sablonnière, 2017), with downstream consequences that depend on whether individuals can integrate perceived losses and uncertainties into a meaningful commitment to change.

This interpretation aligns with emerging evidence that negative affect is not inherently maladaptive. For example, downregulating negative emotions during daily political engagement may improve well-being but reduce collective action intentions (Ford et al., 2023).

Likewise, perceived ingroup threat can motivate action through heightened injustice appraisals and identification (Szóstakowski & Besta, 2024), while framing collective trauma as a challenge has been linked to greater mobilization (Li et al., 2023). More broadly, the BPS-CT framework suggests that experiencing elements of both threat and challenge may facilitate adaptive coping by promoting flexibility and sustained effort (Uphill et al., 2019).

Although no research has yet directly examined how initial threat during hierarchydisruptive social change may evolve into challenge over time, our findings suggest this transition may represent a promising avenue for future research. Future research could track physiological threat and challenge at multiple stages, such as during an initial speech and after reflection, to examine how initial responses evolve and identify conditions that promote adaptive, challenge-oriented engagement. Importantly, this possibility does not minimize the potentially detrimental effects of early threat responses, such as withdrawal, poorer performance and especially detrimental effects on well-being and physical health. This is tentatively suggested by the observation that among concerned moralists, and even more so among ambivalent supporters, many reported that others should take action for change, and some that no action should be taken, consistent with BPS-CT linking threat to withdrawal.

Observations from the collective resilients clusters may suggest how threat could move toward challenge, possibly over time. In particular, collective resources, including trust in collective capacity, some forms of institutional support, and shared responsibility expressed by collective resilients, could play a role in this process, as also shown in research linking perceived collective efficacy to greater engagement in collective action (Bandura, 2000; Lucarini et al., 2025; Uysal et al., 2025). Although support has been identified as a key resource (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010), BPS-CT research has primarily focused on individuals' appraisals of their own demands and coping resources. The present findings suggest that future research should also investigate the role of collective resources in supporting more adaptive responses to hierarchy-disruptive social change.

Centering Contextualized, Minority-Inspired Change

A key contribution of our study is its grounding in a real-world context: an academic boycott campaign. Political boycotts, often initiated by minorities or marginalized groups seeking to challenge entrenched power structures, have a long and effective history within social movements, from their central role in the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa to their influence on climate-justice initiatives and contemporary mobilizations for Palestinian rights (Ayling & Gunningham, 2017; Barghouti, 2011).

Traditional research often operationalizes social change in abstract, depoliticized terms that reflect majority-centered interests (e.g., societal harmony, inclusivity), potentially overlooking the high stakes and emotional tensions inherent in minority-centered social change (e.g., land protection, economic restructuring) (see Becker, 1967). Reviewing previous physiological research, we noticed a mismatch between studies relying on hypothetical scenarios and those engaging participants with more realistic change contexts.

Recent work by Bacchini et al. (2024), including four studies using both self-report and psychophysiological measures, shows that when social change (versus stability) is made salient in the form of discussing gender norms, dominant group members (e.g., men) often experience less distress and fewer negative self-focused emotions, which ironically reduces their willingness to engage in collective action. This seems to align with what we observed in our rationalizing opponent cluster, whose members exhibited mild cardiovascular challenge while expressing opposition to social change and rationalizations. Moreover, physiological data from webcam-based heart rate monitoring revealed lower engagement under social change compared to stability, even as participants reported relatively positive attitudes. This divergence suggests that explicit openness to change may coexist with an implicitly measured lack of engagement, raising doubts about whether stated support would translate into action.

We propose that this abstract intergroup (majority-centered) versus concrete politicized (minority-centered) framing of social change masks one of the points at which support ambivalence emerges: when social change is grounded in the practice of social movements and objectives of marginalized communities, as in the case of the present study, it may become more difficult for some supporters to maintain abstract endorsement without confronting the personal and structural implications of change, some of which they may not ultimately endorse in their more material aspects, or are less able to cope with.

Limitations, Strengths, and Future Research

While the present study offers novel insights into physiological responses to progressive social change, several limitations should be acknowledged.

A first limitation concerns the absence of counterbalancing in the order of the two conditions of state of change. This departs from standard experimental practice, where randomization is typically used to disentangle condition effects from potential order effects, and therefore represents a potential confound. At the same time, if order effects were driving the findings, one would typically expect a more uniform reduction in physiological engagement and in challenge-threat responses consistent with habituation (Hughes et al. 2018). Instead, while participants showed lower physiological engagement during the second speech, their physiological responses also shifted from challenge to threat, alongside higher self-reported challenge, and increased perceptions of both demands and resources. Moreover, as described in the https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd (section 6), even though engagement seemed lower during the second speech task, the results on challenge and threat relevant cardiovascular activity hold when controlling for physiological markers of task engagement (i.e., HR, PEP reactivity). Given the brief and low-burden nature of the tasks (a 300-word reading and a 1minute speech), a fatigue-based explanation also appears unlikely to fully account for these effects. This pattern is therefore more consistent with a threat response to social change than with a generic order effect, although we acknowledge that it cannot be fully ruled out. This design choice was further guided by theoretical and ecological considerations (de la Sablonnière, 2017), according to which social change is inherently evaluated relative to a stable baseline (i.e., the status quo), which serves as a necessary reference point and increased the ecological validity of our findings. Future research should nevertheless replicate these findings using counterbalanced designs to more fully address potential order-related confounds.

Furthermore, our operationalization of demands and resources relied on self-report measures that were relatively broad, capturing general perceptions of effort, uncertainty, and support. These measures did not significantly mediate physiological threat responses, likely because they were collected post-task and may have reflected reflective rationalizations rather than real-time appraisals (Seery, 2013). Future research could benefit from developing more fine-grained, quantitative measures of demands and resources, and potentially aligning with the thematic categories that we identified in participants' speeches. For instance, participants could rate the anticipated impact of a social change on specific domains, such as career opportunities, financial stability, moral integrity, collective efficacy, which may more closely capture the real-time trade-offs that drive physiological threat or challenge responses (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013).

Relatedly, while this study provides valuable insight into how people navigate tensions toward progress and action, it relies largely on qualitative and exploratory analyses. This approach was necessary to access the kinds of conflicts people actually experience (see Dixon et al., 2017), which may be difficult to detect in survey responses that are shaped by socialdesirability concerns or constrained by predefined items. Moreover, because BPS-CT offers relatively limited theorizing on how physiological appraisals operate in real-world systemic sociopolitical contexts, our analyses were necessarily exploratory. Future research could build on these initial observations with more quantitative and hypothesis-driven designs.

Building on our results, future research could examine differences between dominant and minoritized group members in relation to support of social change, within the BPS-CT framework. Although prior work has distinguished between these groups, it has rarely done so in the context of systemic progressive social change. Given that minoritized communities are often at the forefront of movements driving such change, understanding whether and why threat responses arise, and how they can be navigated constructively, remains an important direction for further work, both practically and theoretically, in addition to understanding such responses among supporters. Relatedly, as noted above, it would be valuable to investigate how threat and challenge appraisals unfold over time. Longitudinal designs could clarify whether and how an initial threat response can evolve into a challenge response as individuals mobilize collective resources, reframe status losses, and cope with the uncertainties inherent to progressive hierarchy-disruptive social change.

Conclusion

Across Western liberal democracies, structural violence and individual inaction persist beneath a veneer of progressivism. Although research on the attitude-implementation gap and collective action has documented this contradiction, the motivational (physiological) processes underlying it remain unclear. Drawing on the BPS-CT framework, our findings showed that physiological threat responses to systemic change, here an academic boycott-like initiative, can emerge even when individuals express support. Importantly, these responses were not uniform.

For some participants, threat appeared rooted in unwillingness to relinquish privileges and difficulty reconciling them with abstract progressive values, accompanied by reluctance to act and a tendency to shift responsibility. For others, threat reflected awareness of the discomfort and sacrifice required to pursue meaningful systemic change, paired with mixed responses, both intentions to act and impulses to delegate responsibility. This distinction offers a more nuanced and constructive view of threat: because progressive change is inherently destabilizing, the capacity to engage with and regulate initial responses may help foster more sustained, challenge-oriented action over time. These results extend prior BPS-CT work, which has largely emphasized threat avoidance. Instead, our study hints at the value of confronting, rather than bypassing, the tensions of hierarchy-disruptive social change.

Figure3 examining Hypothesis 2, analysis of speech-coded support for social change, demands, and resources regarding the selective collaboration model identified four distinct participant profiles.

Further

Ambivalent supporters (highest threat responses, struggling to reconcile progressive values with the perceived costs and challenges of social change); concerned moralists (milder threat responses, acknowledging the losses associated with change while reaffirming personal and collective moral commitments to it); rationalizing opponents (mild challenge responses, justifying their opposition to change); collective resilients (strongest challenge responses, expressing moral and material collective resources alongside low demands). Noticeably, collective demands and resources, such as ingroup uncertainty and losses and shared responsibilities, appeared to exert the strongest influence on participants' responses. However, our manipulation of level of change did not work as intended (see Supplementary Materials Chapter 3, section 7), underscoring the need for future research on how personal, ingroup, and system levels of change shape threat and challenge.
